info.text: Erik Erikson's psychobiography of Gandhi, using a nearly forgotten 1918 Ahmedabad textile strike to show how satyagraha -- militant nonviolence -- resolved a lifelong identity struggle into a historical mission.

citations.title: Gandhi's Truth: On the Origins of Militant Nonviolence
citations.author: Erikson, Erik H.

clusters.name: The Psychohistorian's Method
clusters.fact: Erikson organizes the entire book around a single, nearly forgotten labor dispute: the 1918 Ahmedabad textile strike he simply calls the event. He reads it as the microscope through which the macroscopic pattern of a life, and of a nation's independence movement, both become visible. Diagnosing Gandhi as a homo religiosus -- a figure whose private crisis turns out to be representative of an entire culture's unresolved one -- is what licenses a single strike to carry that much interpretive weight. Erikson names his own method disciplined subjectivity: the historian's emotional involvement with a subject this large has to be examined and used, not pretended away.

termInfo.disciplined subjectivity: Erikson's term for the psychohistorian's own method: rather than pretending to stand outside an emotionally powerful subject, the biographer must consciously examine and use that involvement as part of the evidence.
termInfo.homo religiosus: Erikson's category, borrowed from the history of religions, for a figure whose own inner crisis coincides with and comes to represent a whole culture's unresolved crisis. He applies it to both Luther and Gandhi.
termInfo.the event: Erikson's own name for the 1918 Ahmedabad textile strike -- capitalized throughout the book as its organizing case, the single dramatic incident through which he reads Gandhi's whole development.

info.text: Erikson's psychohistorical method: how a biographer studies a single dramatic life event to reveal the psychological and historical forces converging in it.

clusters.name: The Making of the Militant
clusters.fact: Erikson reads Gandhi's South African years (1893-1914) as an extended moratorium: a socially sanctioned delay of adult commitment during which an unresolved identity crisis can be worked out experimentally rather than settled by default. What breaks open in Ahmedabad in 1918 is that moratorium ending -- Gandhi, at 48, finds the historical cause that fuses a private struggle with a public one. Erikson places the shift inside the eight-stage life cycle he had already mapped: developmentally, it is the pivot into generativity, care redirected from private life toward establishing and guiding the next generation.

termInfo.generativity: The seventh of Erikson's eight psychosocial stages: the capacity to care for and guide the next generation, through parenthood, mentorship, or a broader creative investment in the future. Its failure is stagnation.
termInfo.identity crisis: Erikson's term for the developmental task of integrating disparate self-images into a coherent, continuous sense of self; unresolved, it produces role confusion rather than a settled identity.
termInfo.moratorium: Erikson's term for a socially sanctioned period of delay, granted to some individuals, during which normal adult commitments are suspended so identity can be worked out through experimentation rather than foreclosed by default.
termInfo.the eight-stage life cycle: Erikson's model of psychosocial development across the entire lifespan, in which each stage poses a characteristic tension -- identity vs. role confusion, generativity vs. stagnation among them -- to be worked through rather than definitively solved.

info.text: Erikson's model of psychosocial development across the whole lifespan, applied here to explain why a single strike could resolve decades of Gandhi's unfinished identity work.

clusters.name: Truth as Force
clusters.fact: Erikson resists letting militant nonviolence -- his own book's subtitle, and reportedly the term Martin Luther King preferred -- stand as the whole story: it names the attitude and the action but not the spiritual claim behind Gandhi's truth. Erikson's own preferred phrase is the leverage of truth, borrowed from mechanics on purpose. Both readings sit on top of ahimsa, the refusal to injure, and satyagraha, Gandhi's own coinage for holding onto truth as a method rather than a mood.

ahimsa.text: The principle of non-injury or nonviolence, drawn from Hindu, Buddhist, and especially Jain ethical traditions, that Gandhi builds satyagraha on top of.

leverage of truth.text: Erikson's own name for satyagraha, chosen for its mechanical connotation -- the idea that a firmly held conviction can function as a real, active pressure on events, not just a private belief repeated in the same gestures each time.

links.label: Erikson, "Letter to Gandhi," The New York Review of Books, 1969

termInfo.militant nonviolence: The term of Erikson's own subtitle -- and, he notes, Martin Luther King's preferred term -- for the discipline's active, confrontational posture, even though it categorically refuses violence.
termInfo.satyagraha: Gandhi's own coined term, roughly "truth-force" or "holding onto truth," for his method of active, disciplined nonviolent resistance.

info.text: Satyagraha, Gandhi's method of active nonviolent resistance, first deployed at full scale in the 1918 Ahmedabad strike -- and the vocabulary Erikson uses to explain how it applies real force without violence.

bridges.fact: Erikson's claim is that truth, for Gandhi, is not a fixed proposition to repeat but something that must keep proving itself anew in action -- an actuality. The historian's whole diagnostic apparatus exists to locate that kind of force in a life; satyagraha is Gandhi's own method for producing it in politics.

info.text: Erikson's term for the moment a conviction becomes an actual, tested force in shared life rather than a repeated ritual gesture or private belief -- what a psychohistorian looks for, and what satyagraha is built to produce.

bridges.fact: Gandhi's eldest son converted away from his father's religion, struggled with alcoholism, and died destitute within months of Gandhi's own assassination. Erikson's disciplined subjectivity requires him to hold this alongside the generativity he otherwise credits Gandhi with, rather than resolve the contradiction in either direction -- a refusal of hagiography built into the method itself.

info.text: Gandhi's estranged eldest son, whose troubled life and early death Erikson treats as evidence complicating any simple account of Gandhi's generativity.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts describe a choice Erikson makes about his own method, rather than a claim about Gandhi?
lenses.explanation: Disciplined subjectivity and the event are Erikson's own authorial decisions: how he manages his involvement with an emotionally powerful subject, and which single case he builds the whole book around. Homo religiosus is excluded because it is a diagnostic claim about Gandhi's type, not a decision about how Erikson works.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts describe the developmental turning point Ahmedabad represents for Gandhi?
lenses.explanation: Erikson reads Gandhi's South African years as an extended moratorium, a sanctioned delay before adult commitment. The event -- the 1918 Ahmedabad strike -- is where that moratorium ends: identity work turns into a public cause, which Erikson places at the pivot into generativity, care redirected toward guiding the next generation.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts describe how satyagraha actively compels an opponent, rather than the ethical limit it observes?
lenses.explanation: Satyagraha, militant nonviolence, and Erikson's own leverage of truth all name the active, confrontational application of pressure on an opponent. Ahimsa, the refusal to injure, is the constraint the method observes, not the mechanism that does the compelling.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts show Erikson declining to let Gandhi's public triumph settle every question about him?
lenses.explanation: Erikson's disciplined subjectivity obliges him to hold Harilal's estrangement -- the wreck of Gandhi's relationship with his own son -- alongside the generativity he otherwise credits Gandhi with, rather than resolve the contradiction in either direction.

entries.reason: Gandhi's satyagraha, refined through self-suffering rather than domination, is the acknowledged root of King's own agape and redemptive suffering -- watch the same logic operate first at the scale of a nation, then a generation later at the scale of one city.

learningIntroduction.title: Erikson's psychobiography of Gandhi
learningIntroduction.summary: How a nearly forgotten 1918 labor dispute in Ahmedabad became Erikson's case for the developmental crisis behind Gandhi's mature method of nonviolent resistance.

content.text:
In 1969, the psychoanalyst Erik H. Erikson published *Gandhi's Truth: On the Origins of Militant Nonviolence*, a study built around a small, nearly forgotten event: a three-week strike by textile mill workers in Ahmedabad, India, in the spring of 1918. Gandhi, 48 years old and newly returned from two decades in South Africa, mediated the dispute by fasting alongside the strikers -- one of the first full deployments of the method he called satyagraha. Erikson treats this local, largely successful negotiation as the moment a still-uncertain man became the figure the world would later call Mahatma.

Erikson had already coined the term identity crisis to describe the disorienting work of finding a stable adult self, and had proposed an eight-stage life cycle running from infancy through old age. Gandhi's Truth applies that framework to a single life: the South African years as a socially sanctioned moratorium, a period in which a young lawyer could experiment with causes and selves before any commitment became irrevocable, and Ahmedabad as the pivot into what Erikson called generativity -- care redirected from private concerns toward guiding a whole rising generation. Erikson also turns the method on himself, developing what he called disciplined subjectivity: an insistence that a biographer's own emotional engagement with a larger-than-life subject has to be examined and used, not pretended away.
